abstract.p: Tibetan sheep is a primitive Chinese breed valued for its excellent edible quality and high nutritional value. Despite this, limited research has explore dlimited research has explored the relationship between oat silage supplementation level and its impact on the rumen microbiota, muscle metabolism, and subsequent meat quality. This experiment therefore investigated how varying levels of dietary oat silage affect the Tibetan sheep’s rumen: specifically, its morphological development, enzyme activity, fermentation parameters, microbial flora, and muscle metabolites.The study also examined the relationship between these factors and the meat’s edible quality and conventional nutritional traits. The results showed that compared to lower oat silage ratios a hay/oat silage ratio of 5:5 (OS3) significantly enhanced meat tenderness, color, and protein content. A hay/oat silage ratio of 2.5:7.5 (OS4) significantly increased rumen papillae length and butyrate concentration, thereby improving rumen antioxidant capacity and promoting overall rumen growth and development. Further analyses of rumen microbial communities, metabolomics, and correlation demonstrated that the level of oat silage primarily altered muscle glycolysis process, which subsequently affected conventional nutritional components, color, and tenderness. Additionally, the OS3 group increased the abundance of FD2005, UCG-002, Eubacterium_ruminantium_group, and Succinivibrionaceae_UCG-001. Overall, a hay-to-oat silage ratio of 5:5 was optimal, improving both the rumen microbiota composition and muscle metabolic pathways in Tibetan sheep, which consequently enhanced both rumen metabolism and the meat’s edible and conventional nutritional quality.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: The Tibetan sheep is a core species of the alpine grassland ecosystem and is the “all-purpose livestock” essential to the survival of herders on the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau (An et al. 2020). Owing to their unique hypoxic metabolism, efficient nutrient utilization, and robust genetic foundation, Tibetan sheep demonstrate unparalleled survival advantages in the harsh plateau environment, making them an irreplaceable genetic resource (Deng et al. 2023). As a endemic resource and a pillar of local animal husbandry, their well-being is closely linked to the ecological security and livelihoods of highland pastoral areas (Gómez-Miranda et al. 2021; He et al. 2023). They are known for their tolerance to coarse feed, low oxygen, and severe cold, yet under traditional grazing systems, they face a cyclical nutritional bottleneck characterized by being ‘strong in summer, fat in autumn, thin in winter, and lacking in spring‘ (Kuter et al. 2023). Furthermore, the dual pressures of global climate change and increasing grazing intensity, the conflict between grassland ecological carrying capacity and livestock development has become increasingly prominent, directly threatening the traditional survival mode of Tibetan sheep (Li et al. 2016). Consequently, with pasture degradation and the implementation of grazing bans, fully stall-fed systems have become an inevitable necessity.

Oats are globally recognized as a vital forage and food crop in the world (Hou et al. 2022; Pan et al. 2023), characterized by stronger tolerance to saline-alkali environments, drought, cold, and nutrient deficiency stress (Tahir et al. 2022). In recent years, oat forage has become one of China’s major crops due to its high biomass yield and feeding value, and it is widely cultivated in the northern, northwestern, and southwestern regions for its high biomass yield and feeding value (Hou et al. 2021). Utilizing oat forage for silage is an effective method for providing ruminants with high-quality feed year-round (Ma et al. 2025; Xiao et al. 2023). Notably, even in high-altitude cold climates, oat silage accumulates over 15% water-soluble carbohydrates, is rich in beta-glucans, and exhibits a low buffering capacity, establishing it as a highly promising feed resource (Li et al. 2022c; Zhou et al. 2016). Due to its cold tolerance, high yield, and balanced nutrition, oats have become one of the core roughage sources for ruminants overwintering in high-altitude grazing areas (An et al. 2020). As the ruminant farming industry shifts toward cost efficiency and sustainable development, oat silage has gained increasing attention (Harper et al. 2017; Li et al. 2022b). Research has progressed from basic silage preparation techniques to the precise determination of its optimal inclusion level in ruminant diets (Jia et al. 2021; Li et al. 2022a; Liao et al. 2023).

The rumen of ruminant animals is an extremely complex microbial ecosystem, housing approximately 100 trillion microorganisms, including bacteria, protozoa, fungi, archaea, and a smaller fraction of bacteriophages (Xu et al. 2021). Since these microorganisms directly mediate the degradation and metabolism of plant materials, any change in nutrient availability can alter the structure of the rumen microbial community and microbial fermentation patterns (Dijkstra et al. 2020). Identifying rumen microorganisms in samples using 16 S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing can reveal their species composition (Ren et al. 2025). In recent years, there has been growing interest in understanding the potential links between gastrointestinal microbiota and muscle function (Li et al. 2021). Therefore, muscle metabolomics provides crucial information for assessing the nutritional and edible quality of lamb. Additionally, changes in muscle metabolites can reflect interactions among gut microorganisms, playing an important role in evaluating the effects of different levels of oat silage supplementation on meat quality.

Despite this knowledge, the relationship between the level of oat silage supplementation and rumen microbial function, muscle metabolism, rumen morphological development, volatile fatty acids, enzyme activity, meat palatability, and nutritional components in highland-type Tibetan sheep remains largely unexplored (Li et al. 2025; Luo et al. 2025). In addition, the changes in the richness and diversity of rumen microbial communities and their relationship with the meat quality of Tibetan sheep are not well understood (Ma et al. 2023). Therefore, this study employed multi-omics integrative analysis (microbiomics and metabolomics) to systematically investigate the effects of oat silage supplementation levels on rumen microbial community composition and muscle metabolism. This research aims to reveal the interactive mechanisms between rumen microbiota and muscle metabolism under different oat silage supplementation levels and their pathways affecting meat quality. The findings will provide a scientific basis for optimizing the level of oat silage supplementation in highland-type Tibetan sheep diets, thereby improving feed utilization, reducing costs, enhancing meat quality, and promoting the healthy development of the industry.

sec.title: Experimental design
sec.p: A total of 120 two-month-old Qinghai Tibetan sheep with similar body weights (initial body weight 17.51 ± 1.31 kg) and good physical condition were randomly allocated into four treatment groups. Each group had five replicates, with six sheep per replicate. All groups received a Total Mixed Ration (TMR) consisting of 70% concentrate and 30% coarse forage (dry matter basis). The concentrate was pelleted according to the experimental design.The coarse forage comprised hay and oat silage at varying mass ratios to form the four diets: 10:0 (OS1), 7.5:2.5 (OS2), 5:5 (OS3), and 2.5:7.5 (OS4). The sheep were housed indoors under consistent environmental conditions (temperature, light, and ventilation). Animals were fed twice daily at 08:00 and 17:00, with ad libitum access to feed and water. Health status was meticulously recorded, and standard farm protocols were followed for disinfection, epidemicprevention, and deworming. The feeding trial lasted 100 days, including a 10-day acclimation period and a 90-day experimental period. Table 1 details the complete feed composition and nutrient levels.

sec.title: Sample collection
sec.p: Following the 100-day trial, feed and water were withdrawn for 12 h before slaughter, adhering to animal welfare protocols. A total of 24 healthy Tibetan sheep were selected for this study and divided into four groups, with six animals assigned to each group. All sheep were humanely slaughtered according to standard commercial procedures. Rumen fluid and longissimus dorsi muscle samples were collected from each animal. Each sample was derived from a single sheep, with both the rumen fluid and muscle tissue from each individual processed and analyzed as independent biological replicates. A total of 24 independent rumen fluid samples and 24 independent muscle samples were obtained.The slaughter process and subsequent collection were strictly supervised. Samples of the longissimus dorsi muscle (taken from the muscle between the 9th and 11th ribs) and rumen fluid were immediately placed into cryopreservation tubes and snap-frozen in liquid nitrogen for transport, then stored in a − 80 °C laboratory freezer. Rumen fluid was designated for 16 S rRNA sequencing and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) content determination, while the longissimus dorsi muscle was used for metabolomics analysis. Concurrently, rumen tissue was collected and fixed in 4% formaldehyde for histological analysis.

sec.title: Analysis of edible quality and conventional nutritional quality of meat
sec.p: The nutritional quality of the longissimus dorsi muscle, analyzed 48 h postmortem, was determined using established AOAC International methods (2005). Moisture content was determined by complete oven drying at 103 ± 2 °C completely. Crude protein content was calculated using the Kjeldahl method. Crude fat content was determined by the Soxhlet extraction method. Total ash content was calculated by the weight of the inorganic substance left after burning the samples in a crucible at 550 ± 25 °C for 4 h.

After thawing, conventional methods were employed to assess the edible quality of the samples, including 24-hour pH value, shear force, cooking loss, drip loss, and color values (L* for lightness, a* for redness, b* for yellowness). The pH meter electrode was fully inserted into the center of the meat sample; after stabilization, the electrode was left standing for 5 min to obtain a reading. The Warner-Bratzler shear force (WBSF) was measured using a tenderometer. Samples (2 cm × 1 cm × 1 cm)were cut perpendicular to the muscle fibers. Finally, a modified TCP2 automatic colorimeter (L*, a*, b*) was used to measure the color difference of the meat after natural oxidation in air for 15 min. All assessments were conducted in triplicate to quintuplicate to determine the average values (Jia et al. 2025).

sec.title: Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)
sec.p: The rumen fluid was centrifuged for 15 min at 4 °C at 12000r/min. The resulting supernatant was collected, and its antioxidant capacity and digestive enzyme activity were determined using an ELISA kit (Shanghai Yuanju Biotechnology Center, Shanghai, China).

sec.title: Rumen morphology
sec.p: The fixed rumen tissues were paraffin-embedded and sectioned into 3 μm thick slices. Six non-consecutive sections were obtained from each specimen for Hematoxylin-Eosin (HE) staining. Stained sections were examined under an Olympus DP26 microscope. The ruminal papilla length, ruminal papilla width, stratum corneum thickness, and rumen wall thickness were all measured using Image-Pro Plus 6.0 analysis software. Image acquisition was performed using Slide Viewer (SV) software (Zhang et al. 2025).

sec.title: Short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) composition
sec.p: All of the 11 SCFA standards were obtained from ZZ Standards Co., LTD. (Shanghai, China). Methanol (Optima LC-MS), acetonitrile (Optima LC-MS), and isopropanol (Optima LC-MS), along with ammonium acetate, were purchased from Thermo-Fisher Scientific (FairLawn, NJ, USA). Ultrapure water was purchased from Millipore (MA, USA).SCFA quantification was performed at Novogene Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China) using an Ultra-High Performance Liquid Chromatography coupled to Tandem Mass Spectrometry (UHPLC-MS/MS) system (Vanquish™ Flex UHPLC-TSQ Altis™, Thermo Scientific Corp., Germany) was used to quantitate SCFA in Novogene Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China). Separation was achieved on a Waters ACQUITY UPLC BEH C18 column (2.1 × 100 mm, 1.7 μm) which was maintained at 40 °C. The mobile phase, consisting of 10 mM ammonium acetate in water (solvent A) and acetonitrile: isopropanol (1:1) (solvent B). It was delivered at a flow rate of 0.30 mL/min. The solvent gradient was programmed as follows: initial 25% B, 2.5 min; 25–30% B, 3 min; 30–35% B, 3.5 min; 35–38% B, 4 min; 38–40% B, 4.5 min; 40–45% B, 5 min; 45–50% B, 5.5 min; 50–55% B, 6.5 min; 55–58% B, 7 min; 58–70% B, 7.5 min; 70–100% B, 7.8 min; 100 − 25% B, 10.1 min; 25% B, 12 min. The mass spectrometer was operated in negative Multiple Reaction Monitoring (MRM) mode. Mass Spectrometer Parameters: IonSpray Voltage (− 4500 V), Sheath Gas (35psi), Ion Source Temperature (550 °C), Auxiliary Gas (50psi), Collision Gas (55psi) (Huang et al. 2025).

sec.title: 16s rDNA gene sequencing analysis (Rumen microbiota)
sec.p: Genomic DNA was extracted from the rumen fluid of Tibetan sheep using the QIAamp Fast DNA Stool Kit (Qiagen, Hilden, Germany). The V3-V4 hypervariable region of the 16 S rRNA gene was amplified using the forward primer 515 F (5’-GTGYCAGCMGCCGCGGTAA-3’) and the reverse primer 806R (5’-GGACTACNNGGGTATCTAAT-3’). All polymerase chain reaction (PCR) amplifications were performed in a 15 µL reaction volume containing Phusion® High-Fidelity PCR Master Mix (New England Biolabs), 0.2 µM of each primer, and approximately 10 ng of template DNA. The thermal cycling protocol was as follows: 30 cycles of denaturation at 98 °C for 10 s, annealing at 50 °C for 30 s, and extension at 72 °C for 30 s, followed by a final extension at 72 °C for 5 min. PCR products were visualized on a 2% agarose gel after mixing with an equal volume of 1X loading buffer (containing SYBR Green). The amplicons were then pooled in equimolar ratios and purified. The purified products were used for sequencing library preparation. The libraries were quantified using Qubit and assessed for size distribution with a Bioanalyzer. Based on the effective library concentration and required data output, the pooled libraries were sequenced on an Illumina platform (Vanzin et al. 2025).

The resulting paired-end reads were processed using the following bioinformatics pipeline. First, reads were demultiplexed based on their unique barcodes, and barcode and primer sequences were trimmed. Paired-end reads were then merged into raw tags using FLASH (V1.2.11). Quality filtering was performed on the raw tags with fastp (Version 0.23.1) to generate high-quality clean tags. Chimeric sequences were identified and removed using the UCHIME algorithm against the Silva database (for 16 S rRNA gene), resulting in effective tags. Denoising of the effective tags was performed using the DADA2 module in QIIME2 (Version QIIME2-202202) to generate Amplicon Sequence Variants (ASVs). Taxonomic annotation of the ASVs was carried out in QIIME2 using the Silva database as the reference. For sequences with incomplete taxonomic assignments, information was supplemented using the corresponding dmp file from NCBI. To investigate phylogenetic relationships among ASVs, multiple sequence alignment was conducted using QIIME2. The absolute abundance of ASVs across all samples was normalized to the minimum number of sequences for subsequent alpha- and beta-diversity analyses (Zhang et al. 2024).

sec.title: Non-targeted metabolomics analysis
sec.p: Non-targeted metabolomics analysis was performed on meat samples at Novogene Co., Ltd. (Beijing, China) using a Vanquish UHPLC system combined with an Orbitrap Q ExactiveTMHF mass spectrometer or Orbitrap Q ExactiveTMHF-X Mass spectrometer (ThermoFisher, Germany). Samples were injected into Hypersil Goldcolumn (100 × 2.1 mm, 1.9 μm) and separated over a 12 min linear gradient at a flow rate of 0.2 mL/min. The eluents were defined as Solvent A (0.1% FA in Water) and eluent B (Methanol)for both positive and negative polarity modes. The Solvent Gradient operation was programmed as follows: 2% B, 1.5 min; 2–85% B, 3 min.The QExactiveTM HF mass spectrometer operated in both positive and negative polarity modes with the following settings: spray voltage 3.5 kV, capillary temperature 320℃, sheath gas flow 35 psi, auxiliary gas flow 10 L/min, S-lens RF level 60, auxiliary gas heater temperature 350 °C.

Raw data files generated by UHPLC-MS/MS were processed using Compound Discoverer 3.3 (CD3.3, ThermoFisher). This software was used for peak picking, peak comparison, and quantification of each metabolite. Metabolite identification followed the Metabolomics Standards Initiative (MSI) confidence levels. Only metabolites identified at Level 1 (confirmed using authentic chemical standards) and Level 2 (putatively annotated based on spectral library matching) were retained for downstream analysis.False discovery rate control: The screening of differentially abundant metabolites was performed with FDR correction using the Benjamini–Hochberg method, applying a threshold of FDR < 0.05.Database and software versions: Accurate qualitative and relative quantitative results were obtained by matching the data against the mzCloud (https://www.mzcloud.org/), mzVault, and MassList databases. Metabolite identification utilized the KEGG database (https://www.genome.jp/kegg/pathway.html), the HMDB database (https://hmdb.ca/metabolites), and the LIPID Maps database (http://www.lipidmaps.org/) (Bao et al. 2022). The results that the FDR-corrected detailed results are provided in Supplementary Table S1.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: One-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed using SPSS 26.0 software to analyze the phenotypic data (rumen morphological development indicators, rumen fluid antioxidant capacity and digestive enzyme activity, rumen volatile fatty acids (VFAs), muscle edible quality, conventional nutritional components, muscle metabolites, and rumen microbiota). Multiple comparisons were conducted using the Least Significant Difference (LSD) method. All data are presented as the mean ± standard error (SE), and P-value of < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. Spearman’s correlation analysis was employed to examine the relationships between the rumen microbiota, muscle metabolites, and meat quality parameters.

sec.title: Edible quality and conventional nutritional quality of meat
sec.p: Indicators commonly used to assess meat quality include pH value (24 h), meat color, water-holding capacity tenderness (expressed as Warner-Bratzler Shear Force, WBSF). As presented in Table 2, the WBSF, L*, and b* values of the OS3 and OS4 groups were significantly lower than those of the OS1 and OS2 groups. Additionally, the redness a* value was significantly lower than that of the OS1 group (P > 0.05). Conventional nutritional components for evaluating meat quality include moisture, crude fat, and crude protein content. Moisture content was significantly higher than that in the other two groups (P < 0.05). The crude ash content of the OS2 group was significantly lower than that of the other three groups (P < 0.05), however, its crude fat content was simultaneously and significantly higher than that of the other three groups (P < 0.05); the protein content of the OS3 group was significantly higher than that of the other three groups (P < 0.05).

sec.title: Morphological development of the rumen
sec.p: The results of the Hematoxylin-Eosin (HE) staining are presented in Fig. 1A. Significant differences were observed in both ruminal papilla length and ruminal wall thickness across the four treatment groups. Specifically, the ruminal papilla length of the OS4 group was significantly higher than that of the other three groups (P < 0.05). Furthermore, the ruminal wall thickness in the OS4 group was also significantly higher than that in the OS1 group (P < 0.05) (Fig. 1B).

sec.p: As presented in Table 3, the OS4 group demonstrated a significantly higher concentration of butyric acid than the other three groups (P < 0.05). Additionally, the OS2 group’s butyric acid content was significantly higher than that of the OS1 and OS3 groups (P < 0.05).

sec.title: Enzyme activity
sec.p: The results for rumen fluid antioxidant capacity are presented in Fig. 2A. Total Antioxidant Capacity T-AOC, Malondialdehyde MDA, Superoxide Dismutase SOD, Catalase CAT or Glutathione Peroxidase GSH-Px. Conversely, the T-AOC in the OS4 group was significantly higher than that in the OS1 group (P < 0.05), Malondialdehyde MDA, an oxidative stress indicator, was significantly lower in the OS4 group compared to all other three groups (P > 0.05). For Superoxide Dismutase SOD activity, the OS1 group showed a significantly lower value than the other three groups (P > 0.05). sec.title: Rumen microbial flora
sec.p: A total of 8425 ASVs were identified across the four groups, including 3260 common ASVs. The OS1, OS2, OS3, and OS4 groups yielded 1928, 742, 1140, and 1355 ASVs, respectively (Fig. 3A). Alpha diversity analysis revealed the richness and diversity among the groups (Fig. 3B). Chao1 in the OS1 group was significantly higher than in the OS2 group (P < 0.05). Conversely, the Shannon and Simpson indices showed no statistically significant differences among groups (Supplementary Fig. S1). Beta diversity analysis, performed using Principal Coordinate Analysis (PCoA), revealed a clear separation of rumen fluid samples among the four treatment groups (Fig. 3C). At the phylum level, Bacteroidetes and Firmicutes were the dominant rumen microbiota in all four groups, accounted for 46.88%, 40.19%, 48.00%, and 37.01% (Bacteroidetes) and 43.04%, 45.18%, 43.18%, and 47.85% (Firmicutes) in the OS1, OS2, OS3, and OS4 groups, respectively (Fig. 3D). At the genus level, the most abundant was Prevotellaceae, accounting for 34.08%, 18.03%, 29.37%, and 17.47% in the four groups (Fig. 3E, F). LEfSe analysis identified genera specifically enriched in each of the four treatment groups using an LDA score threshold of 3 (Fig. 3G). The OS1 group was significantly enriched with Prevotellaceae_NK3B31_group; the OS2 group was significantly enriched with unidentified_F082; the OS3 group was significantly enriched with FD2005, UCG-002, Eubacterium_ruminantium_group, and Succinivibrionaceae_UCG-001.

sec.title: Muscle metabolomics analysis
sec.p: The metabolic profile of muscle is closely linked to meat quality. Therefore, to investigate the effects of different levels of oat silage in the diet on the metabolic pathways of Tibetan sheep, we a non-targeted metabolomics analysis was performed on the longissimus dorsi muscle. Following the integration of differentially abundant metabolites (DAMs) in the combined positive and negative ion mode, OPLS-DA revealed a clear separation among the treatment groups (Supplementary Fig. 2).

To validate the OPLS-DA models, the PLS-DA permutation tests were conducted. Showed R2X, R2Y, and Q2 values of 0.0, 0.93, and − 0.66, 0.0, 0.95, and − 0.53, 0.0, 0.93, and − 0.50, 0.0, 0.95, and − 0.61, 0.0, 0.94, and − 0.69, 0.0, 0.95, and − 0.65. The consistently high R2Y values combined with the strongly negative Q2 values confirm that the original OPLS-DA models were valid, robust, and not overfitted.

OPLS-DA analysis and PLS-DA permutation test plots indicate that samples within the same group have similar metabolomic characteristics, a phenomenon that may be caused by the addition of different levels of oat silage.

To validate the OPLS-DA models presented in the previous section, PLS-DA permutation tests were conducted. The resulting plots (Supplementary Fig. 3) yielded the following metrics for each pairwise comparison: OS1 vs. OS2: R2X = 0.0, R2Y = 0.93, Q2 = − 0.66; OS1 vs. OS3: R2X = 0.0, R2Y = 0.95, Q2 = − 0.53; OS1 vs. OS4: R2X = 0.0, R2Y = 0.93, Q2 = − 0.50; OS2 vs. OS3: R2X = 0.0, R2Y = 0.95, Q2 = − 0.61; OS2 vs. OS4: R2X = 0.0, R2Y = 0.94, Q2 = − 0.69; OS3 vs. OS4: R2X = 0.0, R2Y = 0.95, Q2 = − 0.65. The consistently high R2Y values (indicating good model fit) combined with the strongly negative Q2 values from the permutation test (where Q2 < 0.0 is desired) confirm that the original OPLS-DA models were valid, robust, and not overfitted.

A total of 1636 metabolites were identified, primarily categorized into five superclasses: “Lipids and lipid-like molecules,” “Organic acids and derivatives,” “Organoheterocyclic compounds,” “Nucleosides, nucleotides, and analogues,” and “Organic oxygen compounds” (Supplementary Fig. 4). An Mfuzz analysis of metabolite abundance trends generated 10 distinct clusters (Fig. 4A).

Differentially abundant metabolites (DAMs) were identified for each pairwise comparison using the following criteria: VIP > 1, P < 0.05, and Log2 Fold Change Log2FC > 1 (Fig. 4B). The number of DAMs identified for each comparison was as follows: OS1 vs. OS2: 32 DAMs (17 upregulated, 15 downregulated); OS1 vs. OS3: 43 DAMs (26 upregulated, 17 downregulated); OS1 vs. OS4: 182 DAMs (126 upregulated, 56 downregulated); OS2 vs. OS3: 49 DAMs (34 upregulated, 15 downregulated); OS2 vs. OS4: 116 DAMs (20 upregulated, 96 downregulated); OS3 vs. OS4: 167 DAMs (96 upregulated, 71 downregulated).

sec.p: Across all four treatment groups, eight common Differentially Abundant Metabolites (DAMs) were identified, including Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP), alpha-Ketoglutaric acid, cis-Aconitic acid, Citric acid, and L-Palmitoylcarnitine. A KEGG enrichment analysis was performed to determine how metabolic pathways were altered by increasing levels of oat silage. The analysis of DAMs for each pairwise comparison revealed enrichment in distinct pathways (Fig. 5A–F): OS1 vs. OS2: DAMs were mainly enriched in “Glycerophospholipid metabolism,” “Choline metabolism in cancer,” “Linoleic acid metabolism,” “Retrograde endocannabinoid signaling,” and “ABC transporters” (Fig. 5A). OS1 vs. OS3: DAMs were mainly enriched in “Pyrimidine metabolism” and “Purine metabolism” (Fig. 5B). OS1 vs. OS4: DAMs were mainly enriched in “Glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism” and the “Citrate cycle (TCA cycle)” (Fig. 5C). OS2 vs. OS3: DAMs were mainly enriched in “Glycerolipid metabolism,” “Vitamin digestion and absorption,” and “Linoleic acid metabolism” (Fig. 5D). OS2 vs. OS4: DAMs were mainly enriched in “Bile secretion,” “Glyoxylate and dicarboxylate metabolism,” “Fatty acid biosynthesis,” and the “Citrate cycle (TCA cycle)” (Fig. 5E). sec.title: Correlation analysis
sec.p: A correlation analysis was conducted between the differentially abundant genera (identified by LEfSe) and a range of phenotypic traits, including rumen morphology, antioxidant capacity, digestive enzymes, butyrate, and meat quality indicators (Fig. 6A). Prevotellaceae_NK3B31_group was positively correlated with T-AOC, butyrate, and fat content. unidentified_F082 was positively correlated with butyrate. [Eubacterium]_ruminantium_group was positively correlated with redness a* and protein content. Succinivibrionaceae_UCG-001 was positively correlated with T-AOC and redness a*. FD2005 was positively correlated with alpha-amylase, trypsin, and redness a*. UCG-002 was positively correlated with SOD, trypsin, redness a*, and WBSF (shear force).

Similarly, correlations were analyzed between the common DAMs (e.g., ATP, alpha-Ketoglutaric acid) and the same set of phenotypic traits (Fig. 6B). Adenosine triphosphate ATP was positively correlated with alpha-amylase, trypsin, redness a*, and protein content. Alpha-Ketoglutaric acid and Citric acid were positively correlated with alpha-amylase and WBSF. Cis-Aconitic acid was positively correlated with T-AOC. L-Palmitoylcarnitine was positively correlated with MDA, fat content, lipase, and ruminal papillae length.

Finally, correlations were examined between the differentially abundant genera and the DAMs (Fig. 6C). Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) was negatively correlated with FD2005 and UCG-002. Alpha-Ketoglutaric acid and Citric acid were positively correlated with Prevotellaceae_NK3B31_group.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This study found that adding different levels of oat silage had a significant effect on the color and tenderness of Tibetan sheep muscle. Meat tenderness (indicated by Warner-Bratzler shear force, WBSF), which to some extent reflects the hardness, cohesiveness, and elasticity of the muscle (Zhang et al. 2022c). In this study, higher levels of oat silage supplementation resulted in improved tenderness (lower WBSF). This may be because the percentage of intramuscular fat positively affects the juiciness and tenderness of meat (Zhang et al. 2022f). Studies have found that to meet Australian consumers’ satisfaction for palatability, an intramuscular fat content of 4–5% is required (Zhang et al. 2022e). In contrast, the results of this study show that our group fed a 7.5:2.5 hay-to-silage ratio (OS2), which best met this standard, paradoxically exhibited poorer tenderness than that of meat fed with hay/oat silage ratios of 5:5 and 2.5:7.5. This result may be due to the specific muscle fiber structure of Tibetan sheep and the changes occurring in the muscle during cooking, which require further research. Meat color is an important factor affecting consumer preference (Zhang et al. 2023). Generally, meat with higher a* values and lower L* and b* values shows better color. However, in the present study, as the level of oat silage addition increased, the a*, L*, and b* values all decreased (Xin et al. 2025). Although the a* value was highest when the roughage in the feed was entirely hay, its tenderness was significantly poorer. Research has mentioned that myoglobin can be used as a selection parameter for genetically improving meat color. The oxidation of myoglobin leads to the formation of oxymyoglobin, which in turn results in an increase in the a* value(Zhang et al. 2022f). This may be one of the reasons for its high a* value. This study revealed an apparent discrepancy between improved tenderness and a reduced meat color a* value, demonstrating that different meat quality traits are regulated by distinct factors. Tenderness is primarily governed by long-term pre-slaughter factors such as intramuscular fat deposition, muscle fiber type composition, and connective tissue properties, all of which are strongly influenced by nutritional status (Zhang et al. 2022d). In contrast, the meat color a* value is more susceptible to acute post-mortem biochemical processes. It depends particularly on the redox state of myoglobin, which is determined by the rate of post-mortem pH decline, ultimate pH, and the oxidative-reductive balance in the muscle(Xu et al. 2025). Within the nutritional gradient of this experiment, increasing the proportion of oat silage likely optimized the energy supply, effectively promoting intramuscular fat deposition and thereby exerting a key positive effect on tenderness. This aligns with the results observed at hay to oat silage inclusion ratios of 5:5 and 2.5:7.5. However, a high dietary inclusion of oat silage may also elevate pre-slaughter muscle glycogen reserves (Martin et al. 2025). This can lead to more intense post-mortem glycolysis and a rapid decline in muscle pH (Martin et al. 2025). The resulting lower ultimate pH can induce denaturation of myoglobin and sarcoplasmic proteins, directly impairing color stability and manifesting as a reduced a* value, which explains the lower values at the 5:5 and 2.5:7.5 ratios. Furthermore, if the increased nutrient supply is not accompanied by a sufficient intake of antioxidants, post-mortem oxidation may be exacerbated. This negatively affects color stability without necessarily influencing tenderness (Pogge et al. 2015). In summary, altering the hay to oat silage ratio in the diet effectively modified tenderness but concurrently introduced factors that limited the expected improvement in meat color. Future research should integrate pre- and post-slaughter multi-omics analyses to more precisely elucidate the mechanisms underlying the interaction between these traits.

As a specific digestive and metabolic organ in ruminants, the rumen is responsible for feed degradation, nutrient absorption and metabolism, and immune responses. Microbial fermentation produces volatile fatty acids (VFAs), microbial proteins, vitamins, and other nutrients (Anam et al. 2023). Ruminal papillae length and wall thickness are key indicators for evaluating its morphological development (Bahramkhani-Zaringoli et al. 2022). In this experiment, when the level of oat silage was highest, the rumen papilla length and rumen wall thickness were significantly higher than in the other groups. This is likely related to the fermentation characteristics of the rumen. Microorganisms in the rumen can produce VFAs (e.g., acetic, propionic, butyric acid) and microbial protein under anaerobic conditions, providing energy and nutrients for the body (Wei et al. 2016). Volatile fatty acids in the rumen contribute up to 70% of the host’s energy requirements (Baldwin and Connor 2017). In this study, the butyric acid concentration was highest in the OS4 group. Ruminal epithelial cells preferentially use butyric acid as an energy source, which promotes their proliferation, differentiation, and maturation (Zhen et al. 2023). This mechanism directly explains the increased papillae length observed in the high-silage groups. A well-developed rumen is crucial for animal health and performance (Islam et al. 2023). Consistent with our findings, other studies have shown that high-carbohydrate silages promote VFA production (Zhu et al. 2021), as they are rapidly fermented by microorganisms. This rapid fermentation and subsequent butyrate production likely explains why the 2.5:7.5 (OS4) group exhibited the greatest rumen morphological development.

Roughage type and quantity are key factors influencing the rumen microbial community and, consequently, its digestive enzyme activity (Zhang et al. 2022a). Amylase activity reflects the abundance and activity of starch-decomposing bacteria (Krogstad and Bradford 2023). Our results showed that $\alpha$-amylase activity increased with higher proportions of oat silage, likely due to the higher starch content in the silage (El-Zaiat and Abdalla 2019; Swanson et al. 2000). Protease activity is essential for protein digestion (Brock et al. 1982; Trotta et al. 2020). The 5:5 ratio (OS3) group showed the highest trypsin activity, suggesting an optimal environment for protein-decomposing bacteria. This finding aligns with the higher muscle protein content observed in this same group. Lipase activity reflects fat-decomposing bacteria (Zhang et al. 2022b). The 7.5:2.5 ratio (OS2) group had the highest lipase activity, which also corresponded to the highest muscle fat content. While high ruminal lipase does not guarantee fat deposition and may even negatively impact it (Mei et al. 2023), the co-occurrence in this study is notable. The exact mechanism linking this specific ratio (OS2) to increased lipase activity and fat deposition requires further investigation. Overall, the 5:5 (OS3) ratio appears optimal for trypsin activity, favoring protein digestion.

The results of this study indicate that an appropriate supply of roughage contributes to maintaining rumen environmental stability and supporting microbial activity, which is consistent with previous research (Li et al. 2025). Such stability is typically reflected in the dynamic balance between free radical metabolism and the endogenous antioxidant system (Baldin et al. 2022). In this experiment, both superoxide dismutase (SOD) activity and total antioxidant capacity (T-AOC) showed an increasing trend with higher dietary inclusion of oat silage. As a key first-line enzymatic defense against oxidative stress (Wang et al. 2021), elevated SOD activity is generally regarded as an adaptive response by the organism to enhance antioxidant protection. However, persistently high levels of SOD and T-AOC may also indicate that the organism is undergoing sustained metabolic challenge, whereby the upregulation of the antioxidant system represents a compensatory response to increased generation of reactive oxygen species (Cheng et al. 2016; Li et al. 2023). This phenomenon resembles the state of “compensatory oxidative stress” observed in studies of high-energy diets for high-yielding dairy cows or finishing beef cattle, suggesting that rapid nutrient metabolism may generally intensify oxidative pressure in the organism (Sun et al. 2023). Interestingly, in the group with the highest proportion of oat silage, OS4 (2.5:7.5), the level of malondialdehyde (MDA), a key marker of lipid peroxidation damage was the lowest. This apparent paradox of “high antioxidant indicators coupled with low oxidative damage” may reveal the complexity of redox regulation. A plausible explanation is that the highly fermentable carbohydrates provided by the high proportion of oat silage may temporarily increase oxidative pressure from metabolic byproducts, thereby rapidly upregulating enzymatic systems such as SOD (a defensive state) (Cheng et al. 2016). Simultaneously, however, they may also enhance the organism’s overall ability to ultimately control oxidative damage—particularly lipid peroxidation—by supplying specific metabolic precursors or altering energy metabolic fluxes, thus resulting in reduced MDA. This aligns with descriptions in some ruminant studies of the dynamic dissociation of oxidative markers during metabolic adaptation periods. Therefore, the pattern observed in the OS4 group may represent an effectively compensated redox state, in which the organism successfully curbs substantial tissue oxidative damage by mobilizing and enhancing its antioxidant defense capacity.

Rumen microorganisms can indirectly influence host metabolism and metabolite deposition, as reported in previous studies (Ren et al. 2023). Consistent with other research, Prevotella was identified as the dominant genus in this study, with its highest relative abundance observed in the 2.5:7.5 (OS2) and 5:5 (OS3) groups. Given that Prevotella is involved in degrading hemicellulose and starch (Shinkai et al. 2022), these dietary ratios may support improved feed digestion and nutrient absorption. Several microbial genera considered potentially beneficial showed relative enrichment in the 5:5 (OS3) group. The [Eubacterium]_ruminantium_group, a known fiber-degrading bacterium, participates in the breakdown of cellulose and hemicellulose (Wu et al. 2023; Yang et al. 2024). Succinivibrionaceae_UCG-001 and UCG-002, which can produce succinate a precursor of propionate important for host gluconeogenesis (Wang et al. 2023; McCoun et al. 2021; Yang et al. 2024). These genera also consume lactate, stabilizing rumen pH and reducing acidosis risk (Oskoueian et al. 2021). Our correlation analysis linked these two genera to muscle protein and fat. Thus, their enrichment in the OS3 group likely promotes host energy metabolism and, as correlated with trypsin activity, enhances protein digestion, leading to the observed increase in muscle protein. The functional information on FD2005 is limited. Multiple studies indicate that FD2005 is strongly correlated with the degradation of cellulose and hemicellulose in the rumen(Arce-Cordero et al. 2022). It is suggested that FD2005 may participate in the breakdown of plant cell walls by secreting enzymes such as cellulases and xylanases, thereby promoting the production of volatile fatty acids (VFAs, e.g., acetate and propionate). Furthermore, its abundance or activity has been associated with rumen fermentation patterns under high-starch or high-energy dietary conditions (Arce-Cordero et al. 2022). We also noted FD2005 (enriched in OS3) correlated with alpha-amylase, trypsin, and meat color, suggesting a role in carbohydrate digestion and muscle metabolism. In contrast, unidentified_F082, often associated with high-fiber diets (Xie et al. 2023), was abundant in the high-silage group (OS4), a finding that may be specific to this diet or sheep species.The abundance of the unidentified microbial taxon F082 within the rumen microbial community structure often varies in association with factors such as diet type, host breed, and growth phase (Jize et al. 2022). It is suggested that F082 may indirectly regulate host energy metabolism and immune function by modulating fermentation patterns—for instance, by influencing the proportion of butyrate (Xie et al. 2023). These observations align with the findings of the present study. The Prevotellaceae_NK3B31_group, belonging to the family Prevotellaceae, is known to be widely involved in protein degradation, peptide breakdown, and carbohydrate fermentation in the rumen(Liao et al. 2024). Certain strains within this group are capable of utilizing non-fibrous polysaccharides such as starch and pectin, and contribute to propionate production via the succinate pathway, which is critical for energy balance and growth in ruminants.Conversely, the 7.5:2.5 (OS2) group had the highest abundance of Prevotellaceae_NK3B31_group, which has been associated with intestinal inflammation (Zhou et al. 2023; Belanche et al. 2023), suggesting this ratio may be detrimental to rumen health. Therefore, the 5:5 (OS3) ratio appears optimal, fostering a microbial community conducive to rumen health and positive growth outcomes.

We selected key Differentially Abundant Metabolites (DAMs) to explain their relationship with the observed phenotypes. Adenosine Triphosphate (ATP) is an end product of glycolysis and aerobic respiration (Luengo et al. 2021). High post-slaughter ATP levels can inhibit key glycolytic enzymes, preventing the necessary drop in pH and resulting in dark, firm, dry (DFD) meat (Zhang et al. 2020; Huang et al. 2023). Thus, promoting rapid post-slaughter glycolysis is crucial for meat quality and safety. Citric acid, cis-aconitic acid, and alpha-ketoglutaric acid are direct intermediates of the TCA cycle (Kassim et al. 2025). Although the TCA cycle stops post-slaughter (Chen et al. 2024), residual enzyme activity can cause these acidic metabolites to accumulate, accelerating the pH decline. A rapid pH drop inhibits bacterial growth and improves meat color (Gagaoua et al. 2021). In our study, the 5:5 (OS3) group had lower levels of cis-aconitic acid and alpha-ketoglutaric acid than the 10:0 (OS1) and 7.5:2.5 (OS2) groups. This slower accumulation of acidic metabolites may explain why the OS3 group had a lower (less red) a* value compared to those two groups. L-Palmitoylcarnitine is essential for transporting fatty acids into the mitochondria for β-oxidation, a process that generates acetyl-CoA and fuels the TCA cycle (Liu et al. 2024; Shen et al. 2020). Its levels were highest in the 7.5:2.5 (OS2) group. This aligns with our correlation analysis, which showed a positive relationship between L-Palmitoylcarnitine and MDA, fat content, lipase, and papillae length. This suggests the 7.5:2.5 (OS2) ratio is most conducive to fatty acid transport and, consequently, fat deposition in Tibetan sheep.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: In conclusion, this study suggests that a hay-to-oat silage ratio of 5:5 (OS3) is optimal for balancing rumen health and improving meat quality in Tibetan sheep. The level of oat silage supplementation was shown to modulate the rumen microbiota and muscle metabolome. These changes were associated with key phenotypic outcomes, including WBSF (tenderness), meat color, ruminal papillae length, and butyrate concentration. It is important to note that the mechanistic pathways linking these microbial and metabolic shifts to the final meat quality traits, as summarized in Fig. 7, are proposed as a working model based on multi-omics correlations and literature inference. This model provides a foundational hypothesis for future research.
